lessons.title: LEFT, RIGHT, MID and LEN
learn: Check lengths of PAN and mobile numbers

steps.say: This supplier list now shows the state code and the PAN hidden inside every GSTIN, plus length checks that catch a GSTIN with a missing character and mobile numbers with the wrong number of digits.
Here's the plan for this lesson.

acts.t:
In this lesson
• LEFT, RIGHT and MID pull characters out of text
• Get the state code and PAN from a GSTIN
• LEN checks the length of PAN, GSTIN and mobile numbers
Practice sheet: S05-01

steps.say: LEFT takes characters from the start, RIGHT from the end, and MID from the middle, starting at a position you choose. LEN counts the characters.

acts.t:
LEFT(text, [num_chars])
RIGHT(text, [num_chars])
MID(text, start_num, num_chars)
LEN(text)
GSTIN = 2-digit state code + 10-character PAN + entity number + Z + check character (15 in all)

steps.say: Open sheet S05-01. Column C has each supplier's GSTIN. The first two characters of a GSTIN are the state code. Click E2.
Type equals LEFT, open bracket, C2, comma, 2, close bracket, and press Return. You get 24, the code for Gujarat, which matches Surat.
Fill down with Command D. Look at Ganga Paper Mills: 09 for Uttar Pradesh keeps its leading zero, because LEFT always returns text.

acts.h: Select E2:E11 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: The PAN sits inside the GSTIN, starting at character 3 and running for 10 characters. In F2, type equals MID, open bracket, C2, comma, 3, comma, 10, close bracket, and press Return.
Fill down. Every supplier's PAN appears. Now look at row 8, Charminar Pharma. That PAN looks odd: it ends in the digit 1, and a PAN always ends in a letter.

acts.h: Select F2:F11 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: LEN counts characters, so it makes a quick quality check. In G2, type equals LEN of C2 and fill down. A GSTIN must have 15 characters, and row 8 shows 14. One character is missing, which is why its PAN came out wrong.

acts.h: Select G2:G11 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Do the same for mobile numbers. In H2, type LEN of D2 and fill down. A mobile number has 10 digits. Row 6 shows 11 because of a leading zero, and row 9 shows 9, so a digit is missing.

acts.h: Select H2:H11 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: RIGHT works from the end. In I2, type equals RIGHT of D2, comma, 4, and fill down. These last four digits are handy for confirming a supplier on the phone.

acts.h: Select I2:I11 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: A classic slip is starting MID one place too early. Retype F2 as MID of C2, 2, 10 and press Return. You get 4AAKFS4821, which includes part of the state code. In Excel the first character is position 1.
Put the 3 back and press Return. The PAN is correct again.
Now fix the source. Charminar's correct GSTIN has 3390 in the middle. Click C8, type the full GSTIN and press Return. The length becomes 15 and the PAN corrects itself.
Here's a quick recap.

acts.t:
Recap
• LEFT and RIGHT take characters from either end; MID starts anywhere
• Results are text, so leading zeros stay
• LEN is a fast check: GSTIN 15, PAN 10, mobile 10

steps.say: Your turn. The fourth character of a PAN tells you the holder type, for example C for a company and F for a firm. In column J, pull it out of the PAN with MID.

acts.t:
Challenge
In J2:J11, return the 4th character of the PAN in column F (C = company, F = firm).
Answer: sheet S05-01 Done

steps.say: In this finished sheet, branch codes come out of invoice references of different lengths, urgent remarks are flagged in any capitals, phone numbers are cleaned, and the middle digits are masked for sharing.
Here's the plan for this lesson.

acts.t:
In this lesson
• FIND and SEARCH give the position of text
• Combine a position with LEFT or MID
• SUBSTITUTE swaps text; REPLACE swaps by position
Practice sheet: S05-02

steps.say: FIND and SEARCH both return a position. FIND is case-sensitive and SEARCH is not. SUBSTITUTE replaces by matching text, and REPLACE replaces by position.

acts.t:
FIND(find_text, within_text, [start_num])  case-sensitive
SEARCH(find_text, within_text, [start_num])  ignores case
SUBSTITUTE(text, old_text, new_text, [instance_num])
REPLACE(old_text, start_num, num_chars, new_text)

steps.say: Open sheet S05-02. The invoice references start with a branch code, but the codes have different lengths: MUM has three letters and PUNE has four. So first we find the slash. Click D2.
Type equals FIND, open bracket, a slash in quotes, comma, A2, close bracket. Press Return and fill down. The slash is at position 4 for MUM and position 5 for PUNE.

acts.h: Select D2:D9 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Now combine it with LEFT. In E2, type equals LEFT of A2, and for the number of characters use FIND of the slash in A2, minus 1. Fill down. Every branch code comes out cleanly, whatever its length.

acts.h: Select E2:E9 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Next, flag urgent remarks. FIND gives a position when it finds the text and an error when it doesn't, so ISNUMBER turns that into TRUE or FALSE. In F2, type equals ISNUMBER of FIND urgent in C2, and fill down.

acts.h: Select F2:F9 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Look at row 3. The remark says URGENT in capitals, but the flag is FALSE. Row 8, with a capital U, is FALSE too. FIND is case-sensitive, so it only matched row 5.
Switch to SEARCH, which ignores case. Retype F2 with SEARCH in place of FIND and fill down. Rows 3, 5 and 8 are now all TRUE.

acts.h: Select F2:F9 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Now the phone numbers. SUBSTITUTE swaps one piece of text for another. In G2, type equals SUBSTITUTE, open bracket, B2, a dash in quotes, and two quotes with nothing between them. That removes every dash.

acts.h: Select G2:G9 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Some numbers have spaces instead of dashes. Wrap the formula in a second SUBSTITUTE that swaps a space for nothing. Retype G2 and fill down. Every number is now ten plain digits.

acts.h: Select G2:G9 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Before sharing this list outside the company, mask the middle digits. REPLACE works by position. In H2, type equals REPLACE, open bracket, G2, comma, 3, comma, 5, comma, and five capital X's in quotes. Fill down.

acts.h: Select H2:H9 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Change an input to see it flow through. The Mumbai invoice has a new contact number. In B2, type 98200 99887 with a space and press Return. The clean and masked versions update together.
Here's a quick recap.

acts.t:
Recap
• FIND or SEARCH gives a position; use it inside LEFT, MID or RIGHT
• SEARCH ignores case; FIND doesn't
• SUBSTITUTE removes or swaps characters; REPLACE works by position

steps.say: Your turn. In column I, pull out the financial year part of the reference, such as 2026-27. It starts one character after the slash and is seven characters long.

acts.t:
Challenge
In I2:I9, return the year part, e.g. 2026-27.
Hint: MID(A2, FIND("/",A2)+1, 7)
Answer: sheet S05-02 Done

lessons.title: UPPER, LOWER, PROPER, TRIM and CLEAN
learn: Fix names typed in random case

steps.say: This customer list was typed by different people, with random capitals, extra spaces and hidden characters. The clean columns on the right fix all of it with five small functions.
Here's the plan for this lesson.

acts.t:
In this lesson
• Fix names typed in random case
• Remove extra spaces with TRIM
• Remove non-breaking spaces and line breaks
Practice sheet: S05-03

steps.say: UPPER, LOWER and PROPER change case. TRIM removes extra spaces but keeps single spaces between words. CLEAN removes non-printing characters such as line breaks.

acts.t:
UPPER(text)  LOWER(text)  PROPER(text)
TRIM(text)  removes extra normal spaces
CLEAN(text)  removes line breaks and other non-printing characters
CHAR(160) is a non-breaking space; TRIM ignores it

steps.say: Open sheet S05-03. The raw data is in columns A to D and the clean versions go in E to H. Click E2.
Type equals PROPER of A2 and press Return. PROPER capitalises the first letter of each word, so the name now reads Rajesh Kumar, but the extra spaces are still there.
TRIM removes spaces at the start and end, and turns a run of spaces into one. Retype E2 as PROPER of TRIM of A2, press Return and fill down to E9.

acts.h: Select E2:E9 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Look at Anjali in row 5. There's still a gap before her name and between the words. These are non-breaking spaces, character 160, which often come from websites and PDFs. TRIM only removes normal spaces.
Turn them into normal spaces first with SUBSTITUTE: replace CHAR of 160 with a space in quotes. Then TRIM and PROPER do the rest. Retype E2 like this and fill down. Anjali Mehra is clean now.

acts.h: Select E2:E9 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Cities next. Row 6 has a hidden line break after Hyderabad, left over from a copy and paste. CLEAN removes it. In F2, type PROPER of TRIM of CLEAN of B2, and fill down.

acts.h: Select F2:F9 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Emails should be lower case with no spaces. In G2, type LOWER of TRIM of C2 and fill down.

acts.h: Select G2:G9 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: For PAN numbers, a common slip is reaching for PROPER again. In H2, type PROPER of D2 and press Return. You get a capital A and a capital D with small letters in between, which is not a valid PAN.
PAN numbers are always in capitals, so use UPPER. Retype H2 as UPPER of TRIM of D2 and fill down.

acts.h: Select H2:H9 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Here's a pro tip. These are still formulas that depend on the raw columns. To keep only the clean text, select E2 to H9, copy with Command C, then on the Home tab open Paste and choose Paste Values.
Click any clean cell and the formula bar now shows plain text. You can delete or replace the raw columns safely.
Here's a quick recap.

acts.t:
Recap
• PROPER for names, LOWER for emails, UPPER for codes like PAN
• TRIM removes extra spaces; SUBSTITUTE(…,CHAR(160)," ") handles web spaces
• CLEAN removes line breaks; paste as values when you're done

steps.say: Your turn. In column I, make a three-letter city code in capitals from the clean city in column F.

acts.t:
Challenge
In I2:I9, return the first three letters of the clean city in capitals, e.g. PUN.
Answer: sheet S05-03 Done

steps.say: Here, address parts in five columns become one clean line for a courier form, and all the delivery cities become a single comma-separated list. Empty parts are skipped automatically.
Here's the plan for this lesson.

acts.t:
In this lesson
• Join text with the & operator
• CONCAT for several pieces
• TEXTJOIN with a separator that skips blanks
Practice sheet: S05-04

steps.say: The ampersand joins two things at a time. CONCAT joins a list of items. TEXTJOIN adds a separator between items and can ignore empty cells.

acts.t:
A2 & " " & B2
CONCAT(text1, [text2], ...)
TEXTJOIN(delimiter, ignore_empty, text1, [text2], ...)
ignore_empty TRUE skips blank cells

steps.say: Open sheet S05-04. Each address is split across House, Street, Area, City and PIN. Click G2.
Type equals B2, ampersand, then a comma and a space inside quotes, ampersand, C2, ampersand, and another comma and space in quotes, then an ampersand.
Continue with D2, the comma and space again, E2, then a space, dash and space in quotes, and the PIN in F2. Press Return and fill down.

acts.h: Select G2:G9 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Look at Nisha in row 3. She has no Area, so her address shows two commas with nothing between them. The ampersand joins blanks too.
CONCAT does the same job with commas between the pieces instead of ampersands. In H2, type CONCAT of E2, a space dash space in quotes, and F2. Fill down to get each city with its PIN.

acts.h: Select H2:H9 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: TEXTJOIN fixes the blank problem. In I2, type equals TEXTJOIN, open bracket. The first argument is the separator, comma and space in quotes. The second is TRUE, which means skip empty cells.
Then give it the whole range B2 to E2 at once, close the bracket, and add the PIN with an ampersand. Press Return and fill down. Nisha's address reads cleanly now.

acts.h: Select I2:I9 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: To see what TRUE is doing, retype I3 with FALSE in its place and press Return. The empty Area comes back as a double comma.
Change it back to TRUE and press Return.
TEXTJOIN also turns a column into one line. In B12, type TEXTJOIN with comma and space, TRUE, and the City column E2 to E9. You get every delivery city in one cell, ready to paste into an email.
Now add the missing area for Nisha. Type Mullick Bazar in D3 and press Return. Both address columns pick it up straight away.

acts.h: Type Mullick Bazar and press Return

steps.say: Here's a quick recap.

acts.t:
Recap
• & joins two items; remember spaces and commas in quotes
• CONCAT takes a list of items
• TEXTJOIN(separator, TRUE, range) joins a whole range and skips blanks

steps.say: Your turn. In column J, build a courier label of name, city and PIN separated by a space, a vertical bar and a space, using TEXTJOIN.

acts.t:
Challenge
In J2:J9, make "Name | City | PIN" with TEXTJOIN and the separator " | ".
Answer: sheet S05-04 Done

checks.equals: Pune, Kolkata, Kochi, Thane, Lucknow, Chennai, Chandigarh, Hyderabad

lessons.title: TEXT and VALUE
learn: Format numbers and dates inside sentences

steps.say: Each row now has a ready-made line for an offer letter, with the joining date and the CTC written the Indian way. The bonus column, which came in as text, has been converted so the total finally works.
Here's the plan for this lesson.

acts.t:
In this lesson
• TEXT formats numbers and dates inside a sentence
• Indian lakh grouping inside TEXT
• VALUE converts numbers stored as text
Practice sheet: S05-05

steps.say: TEXT turns a number or date into text in the format you ask for, using the same codes as Format Cells. VALUE does the opposite: it turns text that looks like a number into a real number.

acts.t:
TEXT(value, format_text)
"dd-mmm-yyyy"  15-Apr-2024
"dddd"  Monday
"##,##0"  85,000
VALUE(text)  "8,750" becomes 8750

steps.say: Open sheet S05-05. We want one sentence per employee with the joining date and monthly CTC. Click D2.
Start with a plain join: A2, ampersand, joined on in quotes with a space on each side, ampersand, B2. Press Return. The date turns into a number. Joining shows a date's serial number, not its format.

acts.h: Type =A2&" joined on "&B2 and press Return

steps.say: TEXT fixes that. Retype D2 with TEXT of B2 and the format code dd dash mmm dash yyyy in quotes. That gives 15-Apr-2024. Don't press Return yet.
Continue with an ampersand, the words with a monthly CTC of and the rupee symbol in quotes, then TEXT of C2 with the code hash hash comma hash hash zero. Press Return and fill down.

acts.h: Type &" with a monthly CTC of ₹"&TEXT(C2,"##,##0") and press Return
Select D2:D9 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Look at Rahul in row 3. One lakh twenty thousand shows as 120,000, the Western style. A normal format code puts a comma every three digits.

For lakh grouping, use a conditional code. In square brackets, greater than or equal to 100000, then hash hash, backslash comma, hash hash, backslash comma, hash hash zero, a semicolon, and the normal code for smaller amounts. Each backslash places a comma exactly where you want it.

acts.h: Type =A2&" joined on "&TEXT(B2,"dd-mmm-yyyy")&" with a monthly CTC of ₹"&TEXT(C2,"[>=100000]##\,##\,##0;##,##0") and press Return

steps.say: Fill down. Rahul's line now shows 1,20,000, and amounts under a lakh, like Aditi's 85,000, still look normal.

acts.h: Select D2:D9 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Now the bonus column, which came from an HR export. The total in E11 shows zero rupees. These numbers are stored as text, and SUM skips text.
In F2, type equals VALUE, open bracket, TRIM of E2, and fill down to F9. TRIM removes the stray spaces and VALUE turns each one into a real number, commas and all.

acts.h: Select F2:F9 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: In F11, type equals SUM of F2 to F9. The bonus total is one lakh fourteen thousand rupees.
The sentences stay live. Rahul's CTC was revised to one lakh thirty-five thousand. Type 135000 in C3 and press Return. His offer line updates with the new amount in lakh format.
Here's a quick recap.

acts.t:
Recap
• Join a date or amount with TEXT, or you'll see a serial number
• Lakh grouping: "[>=100000]##\,##\,##0;##,##0"
• VALUE (or a double minus, --E2) turns text numbers into real numbers

steps.say: Your turn. In column G, show the day of the week each person joined, such as Monday, using TEXT with the code dddd.

acts.t:
Challenge
In G2:G9, show the weekday of the joining date, e.g. Monday.
Hint: TEXT(B2, "dddd")
Answer: sheet S05-05 Done

checks.equals: Rahul Sen joined on 01-Jul-2023 with a monthly CTC of ₹1,35,000

lessons.title: TEXTBEFORE, TEXTAFTER and TEXTSPLIT
learn: Split emails and full names in one formula
Split one cell into rows or columns
lessons.mac:
TEXTBEFORE, TEXTAFTER and TEXTSPLIT need Microsoft 365 (Mac app, web or Windows).
Older perpetual versions such as Excel 2021 for Mac don't have them.

steps.say: In this finished sheet, one formula each gives the first name, surname, email username and domain, even for three-part names. At the bottom, one cell of skills is split across columns and down rows.
Here's the plan for this lesson.

acts.t:
In this lesson
• TEXTBEFORE and TEXTAFTER split at a delimiter
• Count from the end with a negative instance
• TEXTSPLIT spreads one cell into columns or rows
Practice sheet: S05-06

steps.say: TEXTBEFORE returns text before a delimiter and TEXTAFTER returns text after it. The instance number picks which delimiter, and a negative number counts from the end. TEXTSPLIT splits a cell into many cells.

acts.t:
TEXTBEFORE(text, delimiter, [instance_num], ...)
TEXTAFTER(text, delimiter, [instance_num], ...)
instance_num -1 = the last delimiter
TEXTSPLIT(text, col_delimiter, [row_delimiter], ...)

steps.say: Open sheet S05-06. We have full names and work emails. Click C2 for the first name.
Type equals TEXTBEFORE, open bracket, A2, comma, a space in quotes, close bracket. That returns everything before the first space. Press Return and fill down.

acts.h: Select C2:C9 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: For the surname, try TEXTAFTER with a space in D2, and fill down. Ananya's row shows Rao, but Mohammed Irfan Shaikh gives Irfan Shaikh, because it splits at the first space.

acts.h: Select D2:D9 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Add a third argument, minus 1. A negative instance counts from the end, so this means after the last space. Retype D2 and fill down. Every row now shows just the surname.

acts.h: Select D2:D9 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Emails work the same way. In E2, TEXTBEFORE of B2 and the at sign gives the username. Fill down.

acts.h: Select E2:E9 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: In F2, TEXTAFTER of B2 and the at sign gives the company domain. Fill down.

acts.h: Select F2:F9 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Now split one cell into many. B12 holds four skills separated by commas. In B13, type equals TEXTSPLIT of B12, with comma and space as the column separator, and press Return. The result spills across four cells.
To split down into rows, skip the column separator. In B15, type TEXTSPLIT, B12, two commas, then comma and space in quotes. The skills spill down from B15 to B18.
If anything blocks the spill area, you get an error. Type the word note in B17 and press Return. B15 shows the SPILL error, because there's no room for the results.
Clear B17 with the Delete key and the list spills again.
Now edit the source. Add SAP to the end of the list in B12. Both results grow by one cell on their own.

acts.h: Type Excel, Tally Prime, GST returns, Power BI, SAP and press Return

steps.say: One thing to know on a Mac.

acts.t:
Mac corner
TEXTBEFORE, TEXTAFTER and TEXTSPLIT need Microsoft 365 (Mac app, web or Windows).
Older perpetual versions such as Excel 2021 for Mac don't have them.

steps.say: Here's a quick recap.

acts.t:
Recap
• TEXTBEFORE / TEXTAFTER split at a delimiter; -1 means the last one
• TEXTSPLIT spreads text across columns, or down rows with ,,
• Keep the spill area empty or you'll see #SPILL!

steps.say: Your turn. In column G, get the company name from the domain, which is the part before the first full stop.

acts.t:
Challenge
In G2:G9, return the part of the domain before the first ".", e.g. sharmatraders.
Answer: sheet S05-06 Done

lessons.title: REGEX functions: validate PAN, GSTIN and phone numbers

steps.say: This is a vendor master with built-in checks. Every PAN and GSTIN is tested against its official format, the PAN is pulled out of the GSTIN, and messy phone numbers are reduced to ten digits and checked.
Here's the plan for this lesson.

acts.t:
In this lesson
• REGEXTEST: does the text match a pattern?
• REGEXEXTRACT: pull out the matching part
• REGEXREPLACE: remove or swap matching characters
• Reusable patterns for PAN, GSTIN and mobile numbers
Practice sheet: S05-07

steps.say: A regular expression is a pattern for text. You only need a handful of symbols: a caret for the start, a dollar for the end, square brackets for one character from a set, and curly brackets for how many times.

acts.t:
^  start of the text      $  end of the text
[A-Z]  one capital letter    [0-9]  one digit
{5}  exactly five times
[^0-9]  any character that is NOT a digit
PAN: ^[A-Z]{5}[0-9]{4}[A-Z]$

steps.say: Here are the three functions. They need Microsoft 365, on the Mac app, the web or Windows.

acts.t:
REGEXTEST(text, pattern, [case_sensitivity])
REGEXEXTRACT(text, pattern, [return_mode], [case_sensitivity])
REGEXREPLACE(text, pattern, replacement, [occurrence], [case_sensitivity])
case_sensitivity: 0 = match case (default), 1 = ignore case

steps.say: Open sheet S05-07. A PAN is five capital letters, four digits and one capital letter. The patterns we'll use are listed from A13 for reference. Click E2.

Type equals REGEXTEST, open bracket, B2, comma, and the PAN pattern in quotes: caret, A to Z in square brackets, 5 in curly brackets, 0 to 9 with 4, one more A to Z, and a dollar sign. Press Return. You get TRUE.
Fill down. Kaveri Spices is FALSE, because the digits are in the wrong place. Coromandel is FALSE too: it's in small letters, and REGEXTEST matches case by default.

acts.h: Select E2:E9 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: A GSTIN is a two-digit state code, the PAN, an entity number from 1 to 9 or a letter, the letter Z and a check character. In F2, test C2 against the GSTIN pattern from B14, press Return and fill down.

acts.h: Select F2:F9 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Three GSTINs fail. Ganga Paper Mills has an X where the Z should be, Hooghly Jute has only 14 characters, and Charminar Pharma isn't registered at all.

REGEXEXTRACT pulls out the matching part. In G2, extract the PAN pattern from C2, this time without the caret and dollar, because the PAN sits in the middle of the GSTIN. Fill down. Row 8 shows the N A error, because Not registered contains no PAN.

acts.h: Select G2:G9 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Wrap it in IFERROR with Not found in quotes. Retype G2 and fill down again.

acts.h: Select G2:G9 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Now the phones. REGEXREPLACE with the pattern not 0 to 9 and an empty replacement removes every character that isn't a digit: spaces, dashes, brackets and the plus sign.
Wrapping it in RIGHT with 10 keeps the last ten digits, which drops a 91 country code or a leading zero. Close the bracket, press Return and fill down.

acts.h: Select H2:H9 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: In I2, test the result: a first digit from 6 to 9, then nine more digits. Fill down. Hooghly's landline and Malabar's nine-digit number fail.

acts.h: Select I2:I9 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Fix a source value to see the checks respond. Kaveri's correct PAN is AAGCK1259P. Type it in B4 and press Return. The PAN check turns TRUE.
Here's a quick recap.

acts.t:
Recap
• REGEXTEST returns TRUE or FALSE; use ^ and $ to match the whole text
• REGEXEXTRACT pulls out a match; wrap in IFERROR
• REGEXREPLACE(text,"[^0-9]","") keeps digits only

steps.say: Your turn. In column J, test the PAN again but ignore case, so the small-letter PAN for Coromandel passes. Use the third argument.

acts.t:
Challenge
In J2:J9, test the PAN with case ignored.
Hint: REGEXTEST(B2, pattern, 1)
Answer: sheet S05-07 Done

lessons.title: Text to Columns and Remove Duplicates
learn: Fix DD/MM dates that came in as MM/DD
lessons.mac:
Excel for Mac: Data > Text to Columns opens the same three-step wizard, including Date: DMY.
Remove Duplicates is on the Data tab in the Mac app and in Excel for the web.

steps.say: This was a bank statement export with everything in one column and two transactions repeated. Now it's four proper columns, the dates are real dates in the right order, and the duplicates are gone. This lesson is recorded in the Excel desktop app, because it uses the full Text to Columns wizard.
Here's the plan for this lesson.

acts.t:
In this lesson
• Split a bank export with Text to Columns
• Read DD/MM/YYYY dates correctly with the DMY option
• Remove repeated rows with Remove Duplicates
Practice sheet: S05-08

steps.say: Text to Columns is a three-step wizard: choose how the text is separated, choose the separator, then set the type of each column. Remove Duplicates deletes rows that match in the columns you tick.

acts.t:
Data > Text to Columns
Step 1: Delimited or Fixed width
Step 2: the separator (comma, tab, semicolon...)
Step 3: column data format, e.g. Date: DMY
Data > Remove Duplicates: tick the columns that must match

steps.say: Open sheet S05-08. Each line has a date, narration, amount and type, separated by commas, and the dates are day first. Select A1 to A13.
On the Data tab, click Text to Columns. The wizard opens.
In step 1, choose Delimited, because commas separate the fields. Click Next.
In step 2, untick Tab and tick Comma. The preview now shows four columns. Click Next.
Step 3 is the important one. The first column is selected. Choose Date and set the order to D M Y, day, month, year. This stops the second of April from turning into the fourth of February.
Click Finish. The lines split into Date, Narration, Amount and Type, and every date is a real date in the right order.
Here's the mistake this avoids. On a computer set to US dates, skipping step 3 makes 02/04/2026 the fourth of February, and dates after the twelfth, like 15/04/2026, stay as text.

acts.t:
Common mistake
With US date settings and no DMY option:
02/04/2026 becomes 4 February 2026
15/04/2026 stays as text
Always set Date: DMY for Indian bank exports

steps.say: Now the duplicates. The RTGS payment to Indus Auto Parts and the interest credit each appear twice. Select A1 to D13, then on the Data tab click Remove Duplicates.
Make sure My data has headers is ticked and all four columns are ticked, so only rows that match in every column count as duplicates. Click OK.
Excel reports that two duplicate values were removed and ten unique values remain. Click OK. The statement now has ten transactions.
If a statement has already arrived with dates as text, you can rebuild them with a formula instead.

acts.t:
Pro tip: fix a DD/MM/YYYY text date in F4 with a formula
=DATE(RIGHT(F4,4), MID(F4,4,2), LEFT(F4,2))
Year = last 4 characters, month = characters 4-5, day = first 2

steps.say: On a Mac, things are in the same places.

acts.t:
Mac corner
Excel for Mac: Data > Text to Columns opens the same three-step wizard, including Date: DMY.
Remove Duplicates is on the Data tab in the Mac app and in Excel for the web.

steps.say: Here's a quick recap.

acts.t:
Recap
• Text to Columns: Delimited, pick the separator, set Date: DMY
• Remove Duplicates compares only the columns you tick
• Both change data in place, so keep a copy of the raw export

steps.say: Your turn. Cell F4 has a date stored as text. In G4, turn it into a real date using DATE, RIGHT, MID and LEFT.

acts.t:
Challenge
In G4, convert the text date in F4 (15/04/2026) into a real date.
Answer: sheet S05-08 Done

lessons.title: Challenge 4: clean a messy customer export

steps.say: This is a challenge lesson. You get a customer export with fifteen rows, typed in a hurry. Your job is to clean names, mobile numbers and emails, flag duplicates and count the unique customers.

acts.t:
Challenge 4: clean a messy customer export
1. F: name in proper case, no extra spaces
2. G: 10-digit mobile number
3. H: email in lower case, no spaces
4. I: flag Duplicate from the 2nd time an email appears
5. G18: count of unique customers

steps.say: Open sheet S05-09. Names have random capitals and extra spaces, phones mix plus 91, dashes and brackets, and some emails have capitals and stray spaces. The tasks are listed on the right from K1.
Pause the video now and try all five tasks. Everything you need is from this section and the COUNTIF lesson. Come back when you're done or if you get stuck.

acts.t:
Pause the video and try it now.
Check your work against sheet S05-09 Answers.

steps.say: Here's my solution. Task 1: in F2, type PROPER of TRIM of A2, press Return and fill down to F16.

acts.h: Select F2:F16 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Task 2: in G2, REGEXREPLACE with the not-a-digit pattern removes everything that isn't a digit. Don't press Return yet.
RIGHT with 10 keeps the last ten digits. Close the bracket, press Return and fill down. Plus 91 and leading zeros are gone.

acts.h: Select G2:G16 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Task 3: in H2, type LOWER of TRIM of C2, press Return and fill down.

acts.h: Select H2:H16 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Task 4 is the clever one. In I2, COUNTIF counts how many times this email has appeared from the top down to the current row. The dollar signs lock the start at H2, while the end of the range moves as we fill down.
Fill down. Row 6 is Amit Joshi again and row 10 is Neha Verma again, so both show Duplicate. Their first appearances stay blank, which is what you want.

acts.h: Select I2:I16 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: This only works because the emails were cleaned first. Amit's first email in the raw column has a space in front, so it would never match his second one.
Task 5: in G18, ROWS of H2 to H16 counts the fifteen customers. Subtract the number of Duplicate flags with COUNTIF. That leaves thirteen unique customers.
To actually delete the repeats, filter column I for Duplicate and delete those rows, or paste the clean columns as values and use Remove Duplicates on the email column.

acts.t:
Next step
Option 1: filter column I for "Duplicate" and delete those rows
Option 2: paste F:H as values, then Data > Remove Duplicates on Email

steps.say: Here's a quick recap.

acts.t:
Recap
• Clean first: PROPER, TRIM, LOWER and REGEXREPLACE
• COUNTIF($H$2:H2, H2)>1 flags the second and later copies
• Unique count = rows minus duplicate flags

steps.say: Compare your sheet with S05-09 Answers. If your numbers match, you're ready for the dates section.

acts.t:
Check your work
Open sheet S05-09 Answers and compare columns F to I and cell G18.
